blogs.title: The Dog Bite That Didn't Stop: Unmasking Complement-Mediated HUS After Capnocytophaga Sepsis
blogs.description: This post explores the classic 'sepsis masquerading as something else' scenario. We analyze how a seemingly straightforward case of *Capnocytophaga canimorsus* bacteremia evolved into a life-threatening Thrombotic Microangiopathy (TMA). The discussion focuses on the diagnostic tension between Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation (DIC) and TMA, emphasizing why the appearance of hemolysis and thrombocytopenia *after* the septic phase improved should raise immediate red flags for infection-triggered CM-HUS.

blogs.title: Normal C3/C4 Does Not Rule Out Atypical HUS: Navigating the Diagnostic Pitfalls of Complement Testing
blogs.description: Focusing on the laboratory interpretation in TMA cases, this article debunks the myth that normal C3 and C4 levels exclude complement-mediated Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (CM-HUS). We review the specific case where standard complement panels were normal, yet functional assays revealed profound alternative pathway consumption. The post discusses why 'normal' levels can be misleading during acute phases and when to order advanced functional testing (AH50) versus relying on basic screens.

blogs.title: ADAMTS13 is Your Gatekeeper: Distinguishing TTP from Infection-Triggered CM-HUS in Adults
blogs.description: A practical guide on differentiating Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura (TTP) from CM-HUS in the adult population. Using this case as a pivot point, we walk through the PLASMIC score application, the critical role of ADAMTS13 activity (>10% vs <10%), and why waiting for these results dictates whether you start Plasma Exchange alone or bridge directly to complement inhibition. We highlight how a PLASMIC score of 4 helped steer away from TTP in a patient with severe organ dysfunction.

blogs.title: The Eculizumab Paradox: Balancing Complement Blockade Against Active Encapsulated Bacteremia
blogs.description: Addressing one of the most contentious topics in modern critical care: treating active sepsis with terminal complement inhibitors. This post delves into the pharmacodynamics of *Neisseria* and *Capnocytophaga*, explaining why blocking C5 poses a significant risk during active bacteremia. We outline the clinical algorithm used in this case—delaying eculizumab until culture negativity, administering meningococcal vaccines, and maintaining prophylactic antibiotics—to safely navigate the therapeutic window.
